The Nanjing Massacre refers to the mass killing and rape committed by Japanese troops after they captured Nanjing, then China's capital, on December 13, 1937, during the Second Sino-Japanese War. Over roughly six weeks, soldiers killed large numbers of Chinese civilians and disarmed soldiers and raped tens of thousands of women. The International Military Tribunal for the Far East estimated more than 200,000 deaths; China's official figure is 300,000, while some Japanese historians argue for much lower numbers. Iwane Matsui, the commanding general, was convicted and executed in 1948, and Hisao Tani was executed in Nanjing in 1947. China observes December 13 as a national memorial day.
